title: Counting Before Charging: Usage Metering and Rating

know: What a usage event, a meter, rating, a credit balance and a commitment are.

The limits Stripe documents for its meters (events accepted up to 35 days back, a finalization grace period of 1 hour by default and up to 72 hours, cancellation within 24 hours) and the design Stripe described in January 2025 (stream aggregation with a 30-second path and a five-minute durable path).

That Orb's documentation describes the other design (immutable raw events, invoices computed by query), and that Stripe completed its acquisition of Metronome on 14 January 2026 and Adyen its acquisition of Orb on 1 July 2026.
believe: An event that is accepted is not thereby an event that is billed; the two are separate rules.
A duplicate can be removed only by an identifier the producer of the event assigned.
can_do: Write a late-event policy for a usage-priced product: acceptance window, billing cut-off and correction path.
Say whether a requirement needs a real-time balance or invoice-time rating, and what each costs.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given duplicated and late usage in a case the chapter does not contain, the reader says what had to be decided beforehand for each.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An API company bills per request. Its gateway resends a batch after a timeout, so some requests are reported twice. A regional outage then delivers another batch three days after the month ended. For each problem: what must have been decided before the first invoice, and by whom?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Duplicates: each event carries an identifier assigned by the gateway that produced it, so the second report is dropped; an identifier generated on receipt removes nothing. Late batch: whether it is still inside the acceptance window, whether the month's invoice has already closed, and, if it has, which correction path applies (a later invoice, a credit note or an adjustment). The reader distinguishes accepted from billed.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can tell a real-time balance check from invoice-time rating and say which one a prepaid-credit requirement needs.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer has bought €50 of prepaid usage credit. Can the customer use €80 worth before anything stops them? What decides the answer?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Yes, if credit is applied only when the invoice is computed; no, if a balance is drawn down as usage is rated. These are two consistency requirements with different cost, and the chapter gives the documented example of each.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Statements about Orb's architecture are presented as Orb's documentation about Orb, not as facts about Adyen's platform, and no claim is made about Metronome's internal design.

thesis.question: How do you bill for usage when events arrive late, twice and by the billion?
thesis.claim: A usage invoice can stop changing and still be explained only if three time rules are fixed before the first invoice (how long an event is accepted, when the period's invoice closes, how a wrong event is corrected) and duplicates are removed by an identifier the producer assigns; volume then forces one design choice, to aggregate events as they arrive or to keep them raw and compute the invoice by query (raw where prices may change retroactively or an invoice must be explained from its events, aggregated where volume leaves no alternative), and the public record shows one documented example of each: Stripe's 2025 account of windowed stream aggregation and Orb's documentation of invoices computed from immutable events.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that metering is a counter (add one per event, multiply by the price at month end) and that the engineering problem is throughput, to be solved with a faster stream processor.
thesis.so_what: The reader sets the three rules on purpose instead of inheriting a vendor's defaults, knows that a provider can accept an event and still never bill it, and keeps raw events wherever a price may be changed retroactively or an invoice may have to be explained to an auditor.
thesis.how_why: An invoice has to stop changing while events keep arriving, so every usage system draws a line in time and needs a path for what lands after it. Stripe's meters accept events up to 35 days old, bill them only until the invoice is finalized plus a grace period (1 hour by default, at most 72), and allow cancellation for 24 hours; Orb documents a 12-hour grace period and amendments that archive events instead of overwriting them. Aggregating on arrival is cheap to query and loses the original events' context; computing from raw events keeps it and costs more per invoice. Both providers bought their usage engines in 2026 (Stripe completed Metronome on 14 January, Adyen completed Orb on 1 July). Stripe documents Metronome as pushing finished invoices into Stripe one way; Orb's design is documented by Orb about Orb; and the sources used say nothing of Metronome's internals, so the chapter does not place it on either side of the design choice.

supporting_claims.claim: An invoice has to stop changing while events keep arriving, so three time rules must be fixed before the first invoice (acceptance window, billing cut-off, correction path), and an event that is accepted is not thereby billed.
A duplicate can be removed only by an identifier the producer of the event assigned, and only within the period for which the receiver remembers it.

Volume forces a choice between aggregating events on arrival and keeping them raw to compute the invoice by query: raw where prices may change retroactively or an invoice must be explained from its events, aggregated where volume leaves no alternative; Stripe's 2025 post and Orb's documentation are the one documented example of each.
A real-time balance check and invoice-time rating are different consistency requirements with different costs, and prepaid credit that must stop usage needs the first.

Both providers bought their usage engines in 2026: Stripe documents Metronome as its recommended usage product joined to Stripe by a one-way invoice push, Adyen documents no integrated product, Orb's design is documented by Orb about Orb, and the sources used do not describe Metronome's internals.

role.contribution: Shows the time problem in its sharpest form: the amount owed for a period is unknown until a cut-off the system itself must choose, which is where 'late' and 'twice' enter billing before any payment is attempted.

additional_patterns.applies_to: why-counting-is-hard before stripe-meter-rules before two-designs before rating-credits-commitments: the rules, their documented values, the design choice volume adds, then pricing and balances, each using the terms of the one before
scene and in-practice: the unexplained invoice and its repair

flow.rationale: The reader meets a wrong invoice at a trivial volume before any vocabulary, so the rules arrive as the answer to a felt problem and the counter view (throughput is the problem) is set aside early. The rules come before Stripe's values for them, because the documentation is only readable as three separate rules once the frame exists. The design choice for volume comes after the rules, because both designs must implement them and differ in how; rating and credits come after the designs, because the real-time balance depends on the fast path the designs introduce. The acquisitions follow the designs and credits they are the homes of, and the comparison table needs all of it. Larkfield's repair and the failures come last because they apply the rules and their limits. Moving the designs first would present metering as a throughput problem, which is the view the chapter disputes.

hook.content: Studio Noord's plan includes 500 text messages. In March 2027 it sent 1,240. Its invoice from Larkfield charged for 1,324. Of the 1,240, 180 had been reported twice and 96 had been reported after the invoice closed. Three counts of one month (1,240, 1,324, and the 1,144 that arrived once and in time), and each is what some reasonable rule would have billed.

bridge.from_reader_world: An engineer has built counters and knows how to make a stream processor fast; counting things looks like a solved problem.
bridge.to_topic: A bill is a count that has to stop changing and be defensible to the customer, while its inputs arrive late and more than once, so the hard part is deciding in advance what to do with events on the wrong side of a line in time.

thesis_statement.text: A usage invoice can stop changing and still be explained only if three time rules are fixed before the first invoice (how long an event is accepted, when the period's invoice closes, how a wrong event is corrected) and duplicates are removed by an identifier the producer assigns. Volume then forces one design choice: aggregate events as they arrive, or keep them raw and compute the invoice by query. The public record has one documented example of each: Stripe's 2025 account of its meter pipeline and Orb's documentation.

promises.promise: Start from Larkfield's SMS invoice that nobody could explain.
Explain why counting is hard, with the terms usage event, meter and rating and the three time rules.
Read the three rules and the duplicate check in Stripe's meter documentation.
Compare the two designs for high volume: aggregate on arrival or compute from raw events.
Cover rating against versioned prices, credits, commitments and the real-time balance.
Report the two acquisitions of 2026, the status of token billing, and compare the two providers.
Write Larkfield's rules and go through the ways metering fails.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A studio whose plan includes 500 text messages sent 1,240 in March 2027 and was invoiced for 1,324, while 1,144 arrived once and in time, and each of the three counts has a defensible rule behind it.

evidence.what: Larkfield (fictional): Studio Noord, on the €89 plan with 500 messages included and €0.07 per message above that, sent 1,240 messages in March 2027; 180 were reported twice and 96 were reported after the invoice had closed, so the meter billed 1,324 (overage 824, €57.68) where the correct overage was 740 (€51.80).
evidence.shows: The price of the period was not known when the period started, and two ordinary faults (a re-send and a delay) changed it in opposite directions, so the total still looked plausible.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An amount counted from events, like Studio Noord's three counts, is of a different kind from Mila's fixed €120 class pass, which never passes through a meter; Larkfield's own SMS charge to its studios is such a counted amount.

evidence.what: Mila's class pass: €120.00 on Tuesday 9 March 2027 at Studio Noord (scenario ledger). The studio's own bill from Larkfield includes SMS overage at €0.07 per message, billed with Stripe Billing.
evidence.shows: Places the chapter off the payment path but before it: counting happens first, and its result is the amount the payment engine is later asked to collect.

transition_in.carries_over: An amount that has to be counted: the three counts of Studio Noord's month.
transition_in.introduces: Where that sits relative to the fixed-price payment the book follows.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A usage invoice can stop changing and still be explained only if three time rules are fixed before the first invoice and duplicates are removed by an identifier the producer assigns; volume then forces one design choice, to aggregate events on arrival or to keep them raw and compute the invoice by query.

transition_in.carries_over: Three counts of one month with no rule to choose between them.
transition_in.introduces: The rules that choose: an acceptance window, a billing cut-off, a correction path and a producer-assigned identifier; and the design choice volume forces.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter goes from Larkfield's unexplained SMS invoice, through why counting is hard, the three rules as Stripe documents them, the two designs for volume, rating with credits and commitments, the two acquisitions of 2026, the comparison of the providers, Larkfield's rules, and the ways metering fails.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's claim.
transition_in.introduces: The order of the sections.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Larkfield: An SMS Invoice Nobody Could Explain
sections.controlling_idea: Larkfield's SMS meter billed a studio for a count that neither the studio nor Larkfield could reproduce, at a volume of a few events per second, so the question is which rules were never decided and not how fast the pipeline is.

advances_thesis.how: Poses the question in a system where throughput is plainly not the problem, which is the position the thesis takes against the counter view.

flow.rationale: How the charge is set up, what happened to one invoice, then the question it raised; the question only makes sense after the two faults are on the table.

transition_in.carries_over: The claim that rules, not speed, decide whether a usage invoice can be explained.
transition_in.introduces: The company and the invoice that show it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Larkfield charges studios for text messages above a plan allowance through a Stripe Billing meter, fed by a queue consumer, that the growth team built and the payments team took over in May 2027.

evidence.what: Scenario ledger: studio plans at €89, €189 and €349 per month; SMS overage €0.07 per message over the plan's allowance; 'Billed with Stripe Billing since 2018'; the billing integration has 'a meter for SMS usage' and was 'Owned by the growth team, not the payments team, until 2027'. New local facts: allowances of 500, 2,000 and 5,000 messages; Studio Noord is on the €89 plan; its subscription period is the calendar month in UTC.
evidence.shows: Fixes the set-up: who produces the events, which provider counts them, and that the studio is billed on Stripe even though its members pay through Adyen.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ines Bakker's March invoice showed 1,324 messages where her own message log showed 1,240, and the difference was two faults that partly canceled: 180 messages counted twice and 96 not counted at all.

evidence.what: Larkfield (fictional): 1,240 sent; a queue consumer timed out on 17 March and re-sent 180 events without an identifier of its own; the consumer was down from 21:40 UTC on 31 March to 03:20 UTC on 1 April and reported 96 late, after the invoice was finalized at about 01:00 UTC. 1,240 + 180 − 96 = 1,324. Billed overage 824 × €0.07 = €57.68; correct 740 × €0.07 = €51.80; overcharge €12.60, undercharge €6.72, net €5.88.
evidence.shows: Late and twice are ordinary events, they pull the total in opposite directions, and a total alone does not reveal either.

transition_in.carries_over: A meter fed by a queue.
transition_in.introduces: What one month of it produced for one studio.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Larkfield sends about 9 million messages a month, roughly 3.5 per second, so Femke de Graaf's question was not how to count faster but which rules about duplicates, lateness and correction had never been decided.

evidence.what: Illustrative assumption: about 9 million messages a month across 6,200 studios, which is about 3.5 per second on average (9,000,000 ÷ 2,592,000 seconds); Stripe documents a limit of 1,000 meter-event calls per second per account.
evidence.shows: The volume is two to three orders of magnitude below the documented limit, so the invoice's fault cannot be a throughput fault.

transition_in.carries_over: An invoice wrong by two small faults.
transition_in.introduces: The diagnosis that speed was not involved, and the question that remains.

sections.heading: Why Counting Is Hard: The Invoice Must Stop, the Events Do Not
sections.controlling_idea: Usage events arrive more than once and after the time they describe, while an invoice must at some point stop changing, so every usage system has to draw a line in time and say what happens on each side of it.

advances_thesis.how: Defines usage event, meter and rating, and derives the producer-assigned identifier and the three time rules from the way events are delivered.

flow.rationale: The event before the meter that counts it, the meter before the two ways delivery breaks the count, and both faults before the rules that answer them; each paragraph uses the term the one before defined.

transition_in.carries_over: Femke's question: which rules were never decided.
transition_in.introduces: The vocabulary and the two properties of event delivery from which the rules follow.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A usage event is one record that a customer consumed something at a given time, and it needs five fields to be billable: who, what, how much, when it happened and an identifier of its own.

evidence.what: Fields of a usage event with the SMS example: customer (the studio), event name (sms_sent), value (1), timestamp (when the message was sent, not when it was reported), identifier (the message id). Stripe: a meter event includes "the event name configured on the meter, customer ID, numerical value, and a timestamp (optional)" and "an identifier that you can specify in your request" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/recording-usage-api, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: The timestamp and the identifier are the two fields the rest of the chapter depends on, and both are optional in the documented API, which is how they come to be missing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A meter is the rule that turns many usage events into one quantity for a billing period, and rating is the step that applies a price plan to that quantity to get an amount of money.

evidence.what: Stripe: "Meters specify how to aggregate meter events over a billing period. Meter events represent all actions that customers take in your system (for example, API requests). Meters attach to prices and form the basis of what's billed"; aggregation is Sum, Count or Last; after configuration "you can't make any changes aside from the display name" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/meters/configure, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: Counting and pricing are separate steps with separate inputs; the SMS example makes it concrete (count 1,240, subtract 500, multiply by €0.07).

transition_in.carries_over: The event as the unit.
transition_in.introduces: The two steps that turn events into money.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Events arrive twice because any producer that retries after a timeout delivers at least once, and the receiver can tell a re-send from a second real event only by an identifier the producer assigned before the first attempt.

evidence.what: Two text messages to the same member in the same second are two billable events; one message reported twice is one. Their fields are identical except for an identifier created where the message was created. An identifier generated on receipt differs for every arrival and so removes nothing.
evidence.shows: Explains why the belief "a duplicate can be removed only by an identifier the producer assigned" is a matter of information, not of implementation quality.

evidence.what: Stripe: "If you don't specify an identifier, we auto-generate one for you" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/recording-usage-api, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: The documented default is the case in which a re-send cannot be recognized.

transition_in.carries_over: The clean picture: events in, quantity out.
transition_in.introduces: The first way delivery breaks it: the same event more than once.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Events arrive late because the time something happened and the time it was reported are different clocks, while the invoice for the period has to be finalized, after which it may no longer change.

evidence.what: A batch job, a queue backlog, a mobile client offline or a vendor receipt can report at 03:20 what happened at 23:50. The invoice is a legal document that is frozen at finalization (owned by the next chapter). Whatever instant is chosen for freezing it, some event for the period can still arrive after it.
evidence.shows: Shows that lateness cannot be engineered away, only bounded, which is why a rule is needed and a faster pipeline is not an answer.

transition_in.carries_over: Events that arrive twice.
transition_in.introduces: The second property: events that arrive after the period they belong to, against an invoice that has to stop.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three rules therefore have to be chosen before the first invoice (how long an event is accepted, when the period's invoice closes, how a wrong or late event is corrected afterwards), and the first two are different lines: an event can be accepted and never billed.

evidence.what: The three rules: acceptance window (question: how old may an event be and still be stored? if undecided: old events are silently dropped or accepted forever); billing cut-off (question: until when does an event for a period change that period's invoice? if undecided: invoices that keep changing or usage that is never charged); correction path (question: what happens to an event that was wrong, or that arrived after the cut-off? if undecided: manual edits nobody can trace).
evidence.shows: Gives the reader the frame used for the rest of the chapter and separates "accepted" from "billed".

transition_in.carries_over: Duplicates and lateness as permanent properties of delivery.
transition_in.introduces: The three rules they force, and the gap between accepting an event and billing it.

sections.heading: The Three Rules as Stripe's Meters Document Them
sections.controlling_idea: Stripe's documentation gives each rule a number (35 days to accept, 1 to 72 hours to bill, 24 hours to cancel) and says in plain words that an accepted event may never be invoiced; its duplicate check is also bounded in time.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the documented example of each rule and of the identifier, with its limits.

flow.rationale: One paragraph per rule in the order the previous section named them, then the identifier, then the contract as a whole, so the reader can lay the documentation over the frame.

transition_in.carries_over: Three rules stated in the abstract.
transition_in.introduces: One provider's documented values for each.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe accepts a meter event whose timestamp is up to 35 days in the past or 5 minutes in the future, and states that acceptance does not mean the usage will be invoiced.

evidence.what: "Make sure the timestamp is within the past 35 calendar days and isn't more than 5 minutes in the future"; "The 35-day window determines whether Stripe accepts a meter event. It doesn't guarantee that Stripe can include the usage on an invoice ... Stripe might accept an event after finalization and include it in meter summaries without updating the finalized invoice or adding the usage to the next invoice" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/recording-usage-api, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: The acceptance window and the billing cut-off are documented as two separate rules, and the gap between them is usage that is visible in summaries and never charged.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The billing cut-off is the finalization of the period's invoice, which Stripe delays by a grace period of 1 hour by default and at most 72 hours, and which does not apply to every kind of invoice.

evidence.what: "All invoices have a default finalization grace period of 1 hour. During the finalization grace period, you can continue to report usage for the previous billing period"; "You can set a delay of up to 72 hours (3 days)"; only subscription cycle invoices and schedule phase transition invoices include that usage; threshold invoices "reflect only the usage accrued up to the point the invoice is created" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/configure-grace-period, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: The cut-off is a setting the merchant chooses, at the price of invoicing later, and it has documented exceptions.

transition_in.carries_over: The acceptance window.
transition_in.introduces: The second rule: the cut-off after which the invoice no longer takes usage.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The correction path Stripe documents at the meter is narrow (cancel an event within 24 hours of sending it, or offset usage in an open period with a negative quantity), and neither changes a finalized invoice, so corrections after finalization are made with a credit note or a line on a later invoice.

evidence.what: "You can only cancel events sent to Stripe within the last 24 hours. If you cancel usage that's included on a finalized invoice, we won't update the invoice or issue a corrected invoice for the canceled usage"; "You can also fix incorrectly recorded usage data by recording negative quantities. If the overall cycle usage is negative, Stripe reports the invoice line item usage quantity as 0" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/meters/configure, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: After finalization the meter offers no correction, so the correction path has to be built from invoicing tools (a credit note or a line on a later invoice).

transition_in.carries_over: The cut-off.
transition_in.introduces: The third rule: what can be corrected, and until when.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe removes duplicates by the event's identifier and enforces its uniqueness for a rolling period of at least 24 hours, so even a producer-assigned identifier protects only against re-sends inside that period.

evidence.what: API reference, `identifier`: "A unique identifier for the event. If not provided, one is generated. We recommend using UUID-like identifiers. Stripe enforces uniqueness within a rolling period of at least 24 hours. The enforcement of uniqueness primarily addresses issues arising from accidental retries or other problems occurring within extremely brief time intervals" (https://docs.stripe.com/api/billing/meter-event/create, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: Deduplication is itself a time rule: a replay of a three-day-old batch is outside what the documentation promises to catch.

transition_in.carries_over: Three time rules with documented values.
transition_in.introduces: The identifier, and the time limit on it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Taken as a contract, the meter API promises asynchronous ingestion at documented rates and reports invalid events out of band, and does not promise that a summary is current or that an accepted event is billed.

evidence.what: What it promises / what it does not: rate (1,000 calls per second per account, one concurrent call per customer per meter; 10,000 events per second on API v2 streams, 200,000 through sales) / not that a Connect platform acting for a connected account gets more than 100 operations per second; consistency ("Stripe processes meter events asynchronously, so aggregated usage in meter event summaries and on upcoming invoices might not immediately reflect recently received meter events") / not read-your-writes; failure (invalid events reported through `v1.billing.meter.error_report_triggered` and `v1.billing.meter.no_meter_found`, with codes such as `timestamp_too_far_in_past`) / not a synchronous rejection; configuration (a meter cannot be changed after configuration except its display name) (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/recording-usage-api, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: The requirements table the style guide asks for: how fast, how consistent, what happens on failure, each as documented.

transition_in.carries_over: The rules and the identifier one by one.
transition_in.introduces: The same documentation read as one contract with its limits.

sections.heading: By the Billion: Aggregate on Arrival or Compute From Raw Events
sections.controlling_idea: At high volume a metering system either aggregates events as they arrive or keeps them raw and computes the invoice by query; Stripe's 2025 post documents the first for its meters and Orb's documentation the second, and both run a fast and a slow path.

advances_thesis.how: Presents the design choice, the one documented example of each side, where the two resemble each other, and the trade-off.

flow.rationale: The choice, then Stripe's account, then Orb's on the same points, then what the two share, the author's labeled reading, and the trade-off table; the table needs both accounts first.

transition_in.carries_over: Rules that hold at any volume, shown at a few events per second.
transition_in.introduces: What changes when the events come by the billion: where the aggregation is done.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Volume forces one structural decision, where the aggregation happens: at ingestion, by updating counters or windows as events arrive, or at query time, by storing every event and computing the quantity when an invoice is needed.

evidence.what: At 10,000 events per second a month holds about 26 billion events (10,000 × 2,592,000). Summing them per customer at invoice time is a large query; keeping a running total per customer is a small write per event and discards the event.
evidence.shows: Shows why the decision appears only with volume and what each side gives up.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe's January 2025 engineering post describes its meter pipeline as asynchronous ingestion onto an event bus followed by stream processing with Apache Flink, run in two regions at once.

evidence.what: "How we built it: Usage-based billing", Taras Mitran and Karan Dhabalia, 2025-01-28 (https://stripe.com/blog/how-we-built-it-usage-based-billing): events go to "an edge router, which does stateless authentication and API validation, then loads them directly onto an event bus"; Flink chosen for "exactly-once processing guarantees"; "we process the same event in two geographic regions simultaneously"; each event is tagged with "a standardized time stamp, generated before reaching the two Flink applications".
evidence.shows: A documented example of aggregation on arrival, and of what availability costs in a pipeline that must not count an event twice across two regions.

transition_in.carries_over: The choice in the abstract.
transition_in.introduces: Stripe's published account of its side of it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The same post describes two aggregation paths, a 30-second window held in memory for alerts and a five-minute window written to disk for invoicing, and treats the customer's pricing as a second stream matched against the events.

evidence.what: "One is a fast path with a 30-second tumbling window, which we store in memory in real time"; "The second path is slower, with a five-minute window. It's where we write streaming events to disk, in a kind of transactional ledger ... This allows us to accommodate any delayed or out-of-order events"; pricing is turned "into a stream of changes" matched to events "like two sides of a zipper"; a retroactive discount "means opening a lookback window" (https://stripe.com/blog/how-we-built-it-usage-based-billing, 2025-01-28). The post states a capacity of 100,000 events per second; current documentation gives 10,000 by default and 200,000 through sales.
evidence.shows: Late events and retroactive prices are handled inside windows and lookbacks; the post does not describe deduplication, the storage behind the durable path, or whether raw events are kept.

transition_in.carries_over: Ingestion and stream processing.
transition_in.introduces: How the stream is aggregated and matched to prices, and what the post leaves out.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Orb's documentation describes the other design: every event is stored unchanged, and an invoice is the result of a query over the raw events run with the current metric and price definitions.

evidence.what: Orb, "Query-based billing" (https://docs.withorb.com/architecture/query-based-billing, n.d., accessed 2026-11): "Orb's billing engine treats billing as the output of a deterministic query, not a side effect of streaming state mutations"; "Every usage event is stored immutably in a columnar data store. When generating an invoice, Orb executes a fresh query over the raw event data ... The invoice is computed, not retrieved"; on the alternative: "once an event is processed and the counter is incremented, the original context is lost"; "a dependency graph and invalidation system" recomputes only affected invoice fragments.
evidence.shows: A documented example of the raw-event design and of its stated reasons (late events, retroactive pricing, traceability), presented as Orb's statement about Orb.

evidence.what: Orb's values for the time rules: events may be reported "up to 12 hours after the `timestamp`" by default, and in an amendment "Old events are marked as archived"; "Orb never overwrites or permanently deletes ingested usage data" (https://docs.withorb.com/events-and-metrics/reporting-errors, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: The raw-event design draws the same lines in time as the aggregating one, with a correction path that keeps the original events; established here so the comparison table only collects it.

transition_in.carries_over: Stripe's windowed aggregation.
transition_in.introduces: Orb's documented alternative, in Orb's own words.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Orb's documentation also describes a streaming path of running totals used only for alerts, and a pre-aggregating product for the largest volumes, so its design too gives way to aggregation at the top of the range.

evidence.what: Orb: "The stream-based system maintains running totals in Redis (MemoryDB) as events arrive ... But the billing logic never touches these counters—invoices are always computed from raw events" (https://docs.withorb.com/architecture/query-based-billing, n.d., accessed 2026-11); "generally north of 500,000 events per second—and want Orb to pre-aggregate that data in real time rather than storing every raw event, Orb offers a service called "hosted rollups"", default window 10 minutes, partial rollups every 30 seconds (https://docs.withorb.com/events-and-metrics/high-throughput-ingestion, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: Both documented systems have a fast path and a slow path; the difference is which one the invoice is computed from, and volume moves even the raw-event system toward aggregation.

transition_in.carries_over: Orb's raw events and query.
transition_in.introduces: What Orb shares with the streaming design: a fast path for alerts and a rollup product for extreme volume.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Read together, the two accounts differ less in machinery than in what the invoice is derived from (a durable window at Stripe, the raw events at Orb), and Stripe's post does not say whether raw events are also retained.

evidence.what: Inference from the two sources above; Stripe's post does not say whether raw meter events are retained behind the five-minute path.
evidence.shows: Keeps the comparison within the evidence: one documented example of each design, with the limit of the Stripe account stated.

transition_in.carries_over: Two published designs with a fast and a slow path each.
transition_in.introduces: The author's labeled reading of the difference and of what is not documented.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The two designs trade cost per invoice against the ability to reprice and to explain: keep raw events where a price may change retroactively or an invoice must be traced to its events, and aggregate on arrival where volume leaves no alternative.

evidence.what: Trade-off table, aggregate on arrival versus raw events and query, on: cost of producing an invoice; a late event; a retroactive price change; explaining an invoice line; a new metric over past usage; the volume at which it strains; when it is right. Rows are the author's judgement except where Orb's or Stripe's documentation is cited above.
evidence.shows: The trade-off table the chapter needs, with the condition under which each design is right.

transition_in.carries_over: What each design derives the invoice from.
transition_in.introduces: The consequences, criterion by criterion, and the rule for choosing.

sections.heading: Rating, Credits and Commitments: When the Count Meets the Price
sections.controlling_idea: Rating adds two requirements to counting: the price that applied when the event happened, and, for prepaid credit, a decision whether the balance is checked as usage occurs or only when the invoice is computed.

advances_thesis.how: Defines credit balance and commitment and separates the real-time balance check from invoice-time rating, with the documented example of each.

flow.rationale: Versioned prices first because credits are drawn down at a rated amount; the definitions before the consistency question they raise; the cost of each answer last, so the section ends on the trade-off it exists for.

transition_in.carries_over: A quantity per customer per period, however it was aggregated.
transition_in.introduces: The step that turns it into money, and the balances it may be drawn from.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Rating needs the price plan as it stood when the usage happened, so price plans are versioned, and a price that changes in the middle of a period is where aggregated systems document their sharpest limits.

evidence.what: Stripe: "Mid-cycle price changes drop grace period usage ... Stripe skips invoice recomputation during finalization, so any usage reported during the grace period doesn't appear on current or subsequent invoices" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/configure-grace-period, n.d., accessed 2026-11). Orb lists "Versioned pricing objects: Pricing changes are tracked over time" among the inputs of an invoice (https://docs.withorb.com/architecture/query-based-billing, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: A price change and a late event interact: the documented result on Stripe's meters is usage that is not billed at all.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A credit balance is usage paid for or granted in advance and drawn down as usage is rated, and a commitment is a promise of minimum spend over a period, billed as a true-up if usage falls short.

evidence.what: Stripe: "Billing credits are prepaid or promotional usage credit allocated through credit grants. They aren't the customer invoice balance ... or a cash balance, which holds bank transfer funds"; "You can't offer billing credits as stored value to your customers" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/billing-credits, n.d., accessed 2026-11). Orb (early access): a postpaid commitment "settles at the end ... if cumulative usage falls short of the commitment, Orb bills the difference as a true-up"; a prepaid commitment invoices "upfront for a pool of credits that usage draws down" (https://docs.withorb.com/enterprise/commitments, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: Fixes the two owned terms with documented wording, and shows that a billing credit is a prepayment for the seller's own service, kept apart from money balances.

transition_in.carries_over: A rated amount.
transition_in.introduces: The balances and promises a rated amount can be set against.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Whether a customer with €50 of prepaid credit can use €80 worth depends on when the balance is read: at invoice time the answer is yes, with a real-time drawdown it is no, and Stripe's comparison of its two usage products (its basic meters and Metronome, the usage engine it bought in 2026) documents one of each kind.

evidence.what: Stripe, "Compare basic usage-based billing and Metronome": credit-based pricing is "Supported (invoice time)" on basic meters, with the footnote "Credits are only reconciled at invoice time. Customers can exceed their balance during the cycle", and "Supported (real-time)" on Metronome, where "Usage reduces a customer's balance in real time" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/compare-metronome, n.d., accessed 2026-11). Credits page: "Credits apply to invoices only at the time of finalization" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/billing-credits, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: The documented example of each side of the distinction, which is what the prepaid-credit acceptance criterion asks for.

transition_in.carries_over: A credit balance drawn down by usage.
transition_in.introduces: The question of when it is drawn down, with a worked €50 case.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The two answers are different consistency requirements with different costs: invoice-time rating needs only an eventual count and leaves the seller with credit risk, while a real-time balance puts a read of a nearly current total in the product's request path and still overshoots by whatever arrives inside its window.

evidence.what: Stripe's 2025 post: the 30-second fast path "is what we use to trigger billing alerts when someone has spent too much money or is running out of credits"; "P95 latency under 30 seconds for time-sensitive operations" (https://stripe.com/blog/how-we-built-it-usage-based-billing, 2025-01-28).
evidence.shows: Even the documented real-time path is a window of seconds, so "real time" bounds the overshoot and does not remove it; the enforcement decision stays in the seller's product.

transition_in.carries_over: Two times at which the balance can be read.
transition_in.introduces: What each costs to build and what each leaves exposed.

sections.heading: Two Acquisitions in 2026: Metronome at Stripe, Orb at Adyen
sections.controlling_idea: Both providers bought a usage-billing engine in 2026; Stripe documents Metronome as its recommended usage product connected by a one-way invoice push, Adyen documents no integrated product yet, token billing is a preview at one and an intention at the other, and the public record does not describe Metronome's internals.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the dated facts about each acquisition and states where the evidence stops.

flow.rationale: Stripe's acquisition and its documented integration, then Adyen's on the same points, then the use case both cite with its release status, then the limit of all three accounts; token billing needs both owners named first, and the limit applies to everything before it and so comes last.

transition_in.carries_over: Metronome and Orb named as the homes of real-time credits and raw-event billing.
transition_in.introduces: Who owns each since 2026, and how far each is documented as part of its owner's platform.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Stripe completed its acquisition of Metronome on 14 January 2026 and its documentation now calls Metronome the starting point for new usage integrations, connected to Stripe by a one-way push of finished invoices.

evidence.what: Stripe newsroom, 2026-01-14: "has completed its acquisition of Metronome" (https://stripe.com/newsroom/news/stripe-completes-metronome-acquisition). Documentation: "Metronome is Stripe's primary usage-based billing platform and the recommended starting point for all new integrations. Basic usage-based billing, built on the Meters API, is a lower-level primitive that remains fully supported for existing integrations" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based, n.d., accessed 2026-11); "Metronome handles metering, rating, and billing, while Stripe handles payment collection, tax calculation, and revenue recognition" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/compare-metronome); "This invoicing sync is one way, meaning Stripe doesn't send invoice data back to Metronome" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/how-metronome-works-with-stripe); Connect, Adaptive Pricing, Workflows and the Stripe Dashboard are listed as not supported with Metronome (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/compare-metronome).
evidence.shows: Stripe has two usage products with a documented boundary between them: two engines joined at the invoice, not one merged engine.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen announced the acquisition of Orb on 11 June 2026 for $335 million and closed it on 1 July 2026, runs it as a separate product that still serves other payment providers, and has published an intent to converge but no documentation of an integrated product.

evidence.what: Adyen press release, 2026-06-11: "The total consideration for the transaction is $335 million"; "Orb stores the full event stream at scale, decoupling ingestion from invoicing"; "an incubator model, preserving Orb's operational continuity during the first phase of the acquisition and continuing to support multi-PSP environments"; "the strategic intent is convergence" (https://www.adyen.com/press-and-media/jtrg4qd7j3p4rj). 2026-07-01: "Both transactions officially closed on July 1, 2026" (https://www.adyen.com/press-and-media/adyen-closes-talonone-and-orb-acquisitions-announces-leadership-updates). 2026-09-29: "You'll soon see how we bring this unified Adyen and Orb experience to life across our platform" (https://www.adyen.com/knowledge-hub/why-adyen-acquired-orb). No meter, usage or billing object was found in docs.adyen.com as of November 2026.
evidence.shows: On Adyen's side the comparison is with an owned company's separate product; statements about Orb's design are Orb's about Orb.

transition_in.carries_over: Stripe's acquisition and its documented integration.
transition_in.introduces: Adyen's acquisition on the same points.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Billing for AI model tokens is the use case both companies tie these purchases to, and as of November 2026 it is documented at Stripe as a public preview through Metronome and at Adyen only as the stated reason for buying Orb.

evidence.what: Stripe: "Billing for LLM tokens is in public preview and available to all users with a Metronome account"; "Stripe syncs token prices for OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google models"; token type "(input, output, and cached tokens for supported models)" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/token-billing, n.d., accessed 2026-11). Adyen, 2026-09-29: "AI models and modern APIs carry significant, variable compute and token costs" (https://www.adyen.com/knowledge-hub/why-adyen-acquired-orb). Orb commitments are "in early access" (https://docs.withorb.com/enterprise/commitments, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: Separates what is released from what is in preview or early access, and what Adyen has said from what it has documented.

transition_in.carries_over: Two acquired engines and how far each is documented.
transition_in.introduces: The use case both owners cite, and its release status at each.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The evidence stops at three points: Metronome's internal design is not described in the sources used, so the chapter places it on neither side of the design choice; both companies state an intent to unify (Stripe blog post, 23 January 2026; Adyen press release, 11 June 2026) and neither gives a date or says what becomes of the separate engines; and the absence of an Adyen meter is an absence in public documentation, not a statement from Adyen.

evidence.what: Sources read for this chapter: Stripe's documentation pages on Metronome describe the integration and feature tables only; Adyen's three publications state intent; Stripe's blog post of 23 January 2026 says 'we'll build a unified roadmap for one monetization platform' without a date; no docs.adyen.com page on Orb was found.
evidence.shows: Tells the reader which statements in the comparison are documented and which cannot be made.

transition_in.carries_over: What each company has published, including what is still in preview.
transition_in.introduces: What neither has published, and what this chapter therefore does not claim.

sections.heading: Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ
sections.controlling_idea: On metering the documented difference is that Stripe has a meter primitive with published rules, a published pipeline design and a documented acquired engine, while Adyen's side consists of Orb's own documentation and Adyen's statements of intent.

advances_thesis.how: Sets the documented facts of the earlier sections side by side and reads them for an integrator.

transition_in.carries_over: The documented facts about meters, designs, credits and acquisitions.
transition_in.introduces: The same facts in one table, with the author's reading of each difference.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Six aspects separate the two in the public record: the meter primitive, the acquired engine and its integration status, the published design, the time rules, the credit balance, and token billing.

evidence.what: Rows: own meter primitive (Stripe Billing Meters / none found in Adyen documentation); acquired engine (Metronome, completed 2026-01-14, documented one-way invoice push / Orb, closed 2026-07-01, separate and multi-provider, integration "soon"); published design (Stripe 2025 post: Flink, 30-second and five-minute paths / Adyen: not public; Orb's documentation: raw events and query); time rules (35 days, 1–72 hours, 24 hours / Orb's documentation: 12-hour grace period, amendments archive events); credit balance (meters invoice-time, Metronome real-time / Orb documents a credit ledger and early-access commitments); token billing (public preview through Metronome / stated use case, no documented Adyen product). All cited in the sections above.
evidence.shows: The required comparison, each cell a fact cited earlier or "Not public", the last column the author's inference.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An integrator on Stripe chooses between two documented usage products and sets the three rules in configuration; an integrator on Adyen chooses a usage engine as a separate system, Orb or another, and connects it to payments itself.

evidence.what: Orb documents a default event-reporting grace period of 12 hours, configurable per account, and amendments in which "Old events are marked as archived" (https://docs.withorb.com/events-and-metrics/reporting-errors, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: On either provider the rules exist and have defaults; the integrator's job is to choose them on purpose.

transition_in.carries_over: The table.
transition_in.introduces: What to do differently on each provider.

sections.heading: In Practice at Larkfield: Three Rules for the SMS Meter
sections.controlling_idea: Larkfield repairs its SMS billing by choosing the identifier and the three rules on purpose and by keeping its own raw events, and it changes neither product nor pipeline.

advances_thesis.how: Works the March invoice through the frame and shows a late-event policy written for a real product.

flow.rationale: The diagnosis of the invoice, then the policy that would have prevented it, then what Larkfield decided not to build; the policy answers the diagnosis line by line.

transition_in.carries_over: Rules with documented defaults on the provider Larkfield bills with.
transition_in.introduces: The same rules applied to Studio Noord's March invoice.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Laid against the documented rules, the March invoice has two separate causes: the 180 re-sent events carried no identifier of Larkfield's own, and the 96 late events were accepted and missed a one-hour cut-off.

evidence.what: Larkfield (fictional) arithmetic: sent 1,240; duplicates +180; late −96; metered 1,324; allowance 500; billed overage 824 × €0.07 = €57.68; correct overage 740 × €0.07 = €51.80; overcharge €12.60 (180 × €0.07); undercharge €6.72 (96 × €0.07); net €5.88.
evidence.shows: Each fault maps to one rule that had been left at its default: no producer identifier, and the default grace period.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The policy Femke's team writes has four lines: the message id as the event identifier, a 24-hour finalization grace period for invoices with metered prices, cancellation for errors found within a day, and a credit note or a line on the next invoice for anything found after finalization.

evidence.what: Larkfield (fictional), May 2027: identifier = Larkfield's message id; grace period raised from 1 hour to 24 hours for invoices with a metered price (studios are charged a day later); Studio Noord receives a credit note for €12.60 and the 96 late messages are a €6.72 line on its next invoice. Uses Stripe's documented settings (grace period up to 72 hours; cancel within 24 hours).
evidence.shows: A late-event policy is short and every line of it is a choice between a cost and an error; the 24 hours buys coverage of an overnight outage at the price of a later charge.

transition_in.carries_over: Two causes, each a default nobody chose.
transition_in.introduces: The policy that chooses them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Larkfield keeps every message event in its own data warehouse and compares its count per studio with the meter's summary during the grace period, which gives it the raw-event property without a new pipeline or a second billing product.

evidence.what: Larkfield (fictional): the data warehouse holds one row per message (message id, studio, sent-at); a job run during the 24-hour grace period compares the count per studio with the meter's summary and opens an item for any difference. At about 3.5 events per second (assumption) the meter API's documented limit is not approached, and Larkfield sells no prepaid credit, so it stays on meters; Stripe says existing meter integrations "don't need to migrate".
evidence.shows: The choice between the two designs can be made by the customer of a provider as well: the provider aggregates, the customer keeps the events that explain the invoice.

transition_in.carries_over: A policy for late and duplicate events.
transition_in.introduces: The evidence Larkfield keeps so that an invoice can be explained, and what it chose not to build.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong: Replays, Unseen Rejections, Long Outages and Repricing
sections.controlling_idea: With the rules in place metering still fails in four ways: a replay older than the duplicate window, a rejection nobody saw, an outage longer than the cut-off, and a price change that meets late usage.

advances_thesis.how: Gives detection and recovery for each failure of a system that has set its rules, showing that each failure is one of the time limits being crossed.

flow.rationale: From the failure that overcharges customers (the one they notice) to the ones that silently undercharge, ending with the one that depends on a rare combination.

transition_in.carries_over: A policy that works in the ordinary month.
transition_in.introduces: The four ways it is exceeded, and what to do in each.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A batch replayed after the duplicate window has passed is counted again even though every event carries the right identifier, so replays of old data need a check on the producer's side.

evidence.what: Stripe enforces identifier uniqueness "within a rolling period of at least 24 hours" (https://docs.stripe.com/api/billing/meter-event/create, n.d., accessed 2026-11); Orb guarantees "that duplicates are never processed within the account grace period" (https://docs.withorb.com/events-and-metrics/event-ingestion, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: Both documented guarantees are bounded in time, so a three-day-old replay is the producer's problem: record what was sent and acknowledged, and replay only what was not.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An invalid event is rejected after the API call has already succeeded, and the rejection arrives as an event the integration must subscribe to, so an unmonitored meter under-bills in silence.

evidence.what: Stripe: "Stripe asynchronously processes meter events. If we find an error, we create one of the following Events": `v1.billing.meter.error_report_triggered`, `v1.billing.meter.no_meter_found`; codes include `meter_event_customer_not_found` and `timestamp_too_far_in_past` (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/recording-usage-api, n.d., accessed 2026-11). The 2025 post: "when processing does fail, developers don't necessarily know it right away" (https://stripe.com/blog/how-we-built-it-usage-based-billing).
evidence.shows: The failure signal of an asynchronous meter is itself an event that can be missed; detection is a subscription plus the count comparison from the Larkfield section.

transition_in.carries_over: A failure that bills too much.
transition_in.introduces: A failure that bills too little and says so only to those listening.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An outage longer than the grace period puts usage after the cut-off, and one longer than the acceptance window gets it rejected, and in both cases the amount can be recovered only through the correction path.

evidence.what: Stripe: usage reported beyond the grace period is included in meter summaries "but we don't add that usage to the finalized invoice or the next invoice" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/configure-grace-period, n.d., accessed 2026-11); timestamps older than 35 days are rejected (`timestamp_too_far_in_past`) (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/recording-usage-api, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: The three rules are nested limits; each one crossed removes an automatic remedy, and the last remedy is a manual, traceable invoice line.

transition_in.carries_over: Usage lost to a rejection.
transition_in.introduces: Usage lost to time: the cut-off first, then the acceptance window.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A price changed in the middle of a period is the least visible failure, because on Stripe's meters it cancels the grace period for that subscription and late usage for the period is then not billed on any invoice.

evidence.what: Stripe: "If a subscription item's price changes during a billing cycle (for example, because of a mid-cycle upgrade or price update), the grace period doesn't capture late usage" (https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/usage-based/configure-grace-period, n.d., accessed 2026-11).
evidence.shows: A commercial action (an upgrade) changes a metering guarantee; the remedy is to make price changes take effect at period boundaries or to run the count comparison before finalization for changed subscriptions.

transition_in.carries_over: Limits crossed by outages.
transition_in.introduces: A limit removed by a price change.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: Every mechanism in the chapter is a bounded window: the duplicate check, the acceptance of old events, the grace period before the invoice closes, the cancellation of an event, the aggregation window behind an alert. Metering is correct inside those windows by construction and outside them only by policy, so the engineering question is never whether events will fall outside but which window they fall out of and what the written rule is for that case. The choice between aggregating and keeping raw events is the same question asked about the past: how far back can the invoice still be recomputed and explained.
conclusion.so_what: A team that has written its windows down can answer a customer who says "this invoice is wrong" from its own events, and knows in advance which usage it will never bill. A team that inherited defaults finds out both from a support ticket.

callback.to: Studio Noord's March invoice: 1,240 sent, 1,324 billed.
callback.how: The three counts were the same events seen through different windows: with and without a producer identifier, before and after a one-hour cut-off. No number was a bug in the meter; each was the documented result of a rule Larkfield had not chosen.

takeaway.content: Before the first usage invoice, write four lines: who assigns the event identifier and for how long the receiver remembers it; how old an event may be and still be accepted; when the period's invoice closes; and how usage found after that is charged or credited. Then keep your own raw events for as long as an invoice can be questioned.
